title: Cloud+ V4 (CV0-004) practice exam
note: Original questions written for MyNextCert from the public CV0-004 exam objectives (objective numbers follow CompTIA's objectives document). Not real exam questions. Practice in your own free-tier or lab accounts, never with work data or a government card.

q.q: A team wants to run its own custom code but not patch operating systems or manage servers, and it's fine with a provider's runtime. Which service model fits?
o: Colocation of its own servers in a provider's rack
Colocation means managing your own hardware.
PaaS
Right. The provider runs the OS and runtime; the team brings code and data.
IaaS virtual machines with a hardened image
With IaaS the team would still patch the OS.
SaaS from a vendor that hosts a ready-made app
SaaS is a finished app; the team can't run its own code.

q.q: Under the shared responsibility model for SaaS email, which task stays with the customer?
o: Securing the hypervisor that hosts the mail platform
The provider handles the virtualization layer.
Managing user accounts, MFA and data sharing settings
Right. In SaaS the customer still owns identities, access and its data.
Replacing failed disks in the provider's data center
Physical hardware is always the provider's.
Patching the mail servers' operating systems and the mail software
The SaaS provider patches its own servers and software.

q.q: A function must run only when a file lands in storage, for a few seconds each time, with no servers to manage and billing per run. Which model fits?
o: IaaS with a small VM left running all day
A VM runs and bills all the time, and you manage it.
A private cloud cluster of bare-metal hosts
That means owning and managing servers.
SaaS file-sharing app with built-in triggers
SaaS doesn't run your custom code.
FaaS (serverless functions)
Right. Functions run on events and bill per execution.

q.q: An app must survive the loss of one data center inside a region with almost no downtime. What is the simplest design?
o: Take daily snapshots and restore them in a new region if a data center fails
That's a slow DR plan, not near-zero downtime.
Run every instance in one zone on larger VM sizes with faster disks
Bigger VMs in one zone still fail with that zone.
Put the app behind a CDN and leave the origin in one zone
A CDN caches content; the dynamic origin still fails with the zone.
Run instances in two or more availability zones behind a load balancer
Right. Zones are separate data centers in a region; spreading across them survives one failing.

q.q: A business can lose at most 15 minutes of data and must be back online within 4 hours. Which pair describes these targets?
o: RPO 15 minutes, RTO 4 hours
Right. RPO is how much data you can lose; RTO is how long you can be down.
RTO 15 minutes, RPO 4 hours
Reversed: the data loss limit is the RPO.
SLA 15 minutes, SLO 4 hours
Those are agreements and goals, not recovery targets.
MTBF 15 minutes, MTTR 4 hours
MTBF and MTTR describe reliability and repair, not business targets.

q.q: An on-premises app usually runs fine but needs extra capacity during a yearly sale. The company sends overflow traffic to a public cloud only during the peak. What is this called?
o: Lift and shift migration
That moves the whole app permanently.
Cloud bursting
Right. Workloads overflow to the cloud when local capacity runs out.
A warm disaster recovery site
A DR site is for failures, not peak demand.
Edge computing
Edge computing processes data near the users or devices.

q.q: A disaster recovery site has hardware and recent data copies, but needs a few hours to start services. What type of site is this?
o: A cold site with power and space only
A cold site has no ready systems or data.
A hot site that mirrors production
A hot site takes over almost instantly.
An edge site near the users
Edge sites aren't a DR category.
A warm site
Right. Warm sites have equipment and some data ready; they need time to bring services up.

q.q: A company needs a private, consistent-bandwidth link from its data center to its cloud provider, not over the internet. What should it order?
o: Public IP addresses on every cloud server
That exposes servers instead of linking privately.
A site-to-site IPsec VPN over the internet with two tunnels
A VPN is encrypted but still rides the internet, so performance varies.
A CDN with origin shield turned on
A CDN caches content for users; it isn't a private link.
A dedicated connection (direct connect / interconnect)
Right. A private circuit gives steady bandwidth and latency outside the internet.

q.q: Private subnet servers must download patches from the internet but must not accept any inbound connections from it. What should be added?
o: A load balancer listening on port 443 in the public subnet
That's for inbound traffic to the servers.
An internet gateway with public IPs on every server
Public IPs allow inbound connections.
A NAT gateway with a route from the private subnet
Right. NAT lets outbound connections out and replies back, but blocks new inbound connections.
A VPC peering link to a public subnet
Peering connects VPCs; it doesn't provide internet access.

q.q: Two VPCs in the same cloud account need to talk privately with no internet path. Each has a unique CIDR range. What is the simplest option?
o: A NAT gateway in each VPC
NAT is for internet access, not VPC-to-VPC routing.
A CDN distribution with each VPC set as an origin
CDNs serve content to users; they don't route private traffic between VPCs.
A public load balancer in each VPC
That sends traffic over public endpoints.
VPC peering with routes in both VPCs
Right. Peering connects the two networks privately; each side needs a route.

q.q: Logs must be kept for seven years for audits and are almost never read. Which storage tier costs least?
o: Archive (cold) object storage
Right. Archive tiers are cheapest to store; retrieval is slower and costs more, which is fine for rare reads.
A file share on premium SSDs
Premium file storage is for active use.
Provisioned IOPS block storage
Block storage with high IOPS is the most expensive for idle data.
Hot object storage
Hot tiers cost more per GB because they're built for frequent access.

q.q: A database VM needs low-latency storage that it formats with its own file system. Which type fits?
o: Object storage accessed by HTTP API
Object storage isn't mounted as a disk with a file system.
A CDN edge cache in front of the database
A CDN caches content for users.
An archive tier for backups
Archive storage is slow to retrieve.
Block storage
Right. Block volumes attach to a VM like a disk; the OS formats them.

q.q: Many Linux VMs need to read and write the same folder of shared files at the same time. Which storage fits?
o: Instance-local ephemeral disks
Each VM's local disk is private and lost when it stops.
File storage (NFS/SMB share)
Right. File storage is built for shared access through a file system protocol.
Archive object storage
Too slow and not mountable as a shared folder.
One block volume attached to every VM
Most block volumes attach to one VM; sharing them can corrupt the file system.

q.q: An order service calls inventory, billing and email directly. When email is slow, orders fail. Which design change fixes this?
o: Add more retries in the order service with no limit
Unlimited retries pile up and make the outage worse.
Merge all four services into one large application
That tightens coupling and makes failures spread.
Give the order service a bigger VM size and more worker threads
The slow dependency is email, not order capacity.
Put a message queue between orders and the email service
Right. Loose coupling lets orders finish while email catches up from the queue.

q.q: One upload event must trigger thumbnail creation, virus scanning and indexing at the same time. Which pattern fits?
o: A cron job that runs all three steps every hour
That adds delay and isn't event-driven.
A single queue read by one worker in order
That processes the steps one at a time.
Fan-out through a pub/sub topic
Right. One message is delivered to several subscribers that work in parallel.
A larger database to store the uploads
Storage size doesn't trigger the steps.

q.q: Microservices keep breaking because IP addresses change when containers restart. What should the design use?
o: A larger subnet so IPs never change
Subnet size doesn't stop IPs from changing.
Hard-coded IP addresses updated by hand after each restart
That's exactly what keeps breaking.
Static public IPs on every container
That exposes containers and doesn't scale.
Service discovery so services find each other by name
Right. A registry or DNS-based discovery tracks where each service is running now.

q.q: A container writes uploaded files to its own file system. After a restart, the files are gone. What is the fix?
o: Restart the container less often and keep it running longer
The data would still be lost on the next restart.
Mount a persistent volume for the upload folder
Right. Container file systems are ephemeral; persistent volumes survive restarts.
Run the container as root
Running as root doesn't change persistence and is risky.
Use a larger container image
Image size doesn't make runtime data persistent.

q.q: A container listens on port 8080 inside, but users must reach it on port 80 of the host. What is configured?
o: A VPN between the host and the container
Not needed on the same host.
A DNS CNAME from port 80 to port 8080
DNS records don't map ports.
A new image built with the app's port changed
Possible, but mapping is the standard way and needs no rebuild.
Port mapping from host 80 to container 8080
Right. Port mapping forwards traffic from a host port to the container's port.

q.q: Where should a team store approved, scanned container images so every cluster pulls the same version?
o: A private image registry
Right. A registry stores versioned images that clusters pull from.
An object storage bucket of tar files with no index
That loses tagging, scanning and pull support.
Each developer's laptop
Laptops aren't a reliable, controlled source.
Inside the Kubernetes etcd database
etcd stores cluster state, not images.

q.q: Two VMs run the primary and backup of a database. If they land on the same physical host, one host failure takes both down. What should be set?
o: Affinity rules so the two VMs always share the same host
That makes the single point of failure guaranteed.
Larger memory reservations on both VMs
Memory doesn't decide which host they run on.
Anti-affinity rules so the VMs run on different hosts
Right. Anti-affinity keeps related VMs apart so one host failure doesn't take out both.
Thin provisioning on both VMs' disks
That affects storage allocation, not placement.

q.q: A VM needs direct access to a physical GPU for machine learning training at full speed. Which feature allows this?
o: Memory ballooning
Ballooning reclaims memory from VMs.
VM cloning from a template
Cloning copies a VM; it doesn't give hardware access.
Hardware pass-through
Right. The physical device is handed directly to the VM.
An overlay network
Overlays are virtual networks, not device access.

q.q: An admin needs 20 identical test VMs from a configured template in minutes. What should they use?
o: Installing the OS by hand on each VM
Slow and inconsistent.
Cloning from a template or golden image
Right. Clones copy a prepared VM so every copy matches.
Live migration of the template VM to 20 hosts
Migration moves a VM; it doesn't copy it.
Hardware pass-through for each VM
That shares a device, not a configuration.

q.q: Finance can't tell which department is running up the cloud bill. What should the cloud team enforce first?
o: Monthly invoices printed and emailed to finance
Invoices still show one total without allocation.
Smaller VM sizes for every workload
That may cut cost but doesn't show who spends what.
Mandatory cost allocation tags on every resource
Right. Tags like department and project let billing reports split costs.
Move every department into one shared billing account
That hides ownership even more.

q.q: A batch job can be stopped and restarted at any time and needs to be as cheap as possible. Which pricing fits?
o: Reserved instances for three years
Reservations suit steady 24/7 workloads.
Spot (preemptible) instances
Right. Spot capacity is heavily discounted but can be taken back, which an interruptible job tolerates.
On-demand instances running all month
Flexible, but the most expensive per hour.
Dedicated hosts with per-host billing
Dedicated hosts cost more.

q.q: Monitoring shows a group of VMs averaging 8% CPU and 20% memory for months. What should the team do?
o: Add more VMs to the group to spread the load
There's no load problem.
Move them to a faster storage tier
Storage isn't the issue.
Rightsize them to smaller instance types
Right. Rightsizing matches size to real usage and cuts cost.
Buy reserved instances for the current sizes
That locks in paying for unused capacity.

q.q: A shopping app stores orders with strict relationships and needs multi-row transactions. Which database type fits?
o: A time-series database for metrics
Built for time-stamped measurements.
An object storage bucket of JSON files
No query engine or transactions.
A relational (SQL) database
Right. Relational databases enforce schemas, relationships and ACID transactions.
A key-value store with no transactions
No multi-row transactions or joins.

q.q: A team doesn't want to patch database servers, run backups or set up replication. Which option fits?
o: A file share with CSV files
That isn't a database service.
A provider-managed database service
Right. The provider handles patching, backups and replication.
A self-managed database on IaaS VMs
The team would handle all of it.
A database on a developer's laptop
Not suitable for production.

q.q: An app stores user profiles whose fields differ from user to user and change often. Which database type fits best?
o: A relational database with a fixed schema
Frequent schema changes are hard on fixed schemas.
Block storage formatted with NTFS
That's storage, not a database.
A data warehouse for analytics
Warehouses are for reporting, not app profiles.
A document (NoSQL) database
Right. Document stores handle flexible, changing structures well.

q.q: A database VM is slow, and monitoring shows disk queue length is high while CPU is low. What should be increased?
o: Network bandwidth to the internet
The issue is local disk activity.
Storage IOPS
Right. The bottleneck is the disk, so more IOPS helps.
The VM's DNS cache size
DNS has nothing to do with disk waits.
vCPU count
CPU is idle; more of it won't help.

q.q: A machine learning training job needs massive parallel math. Which compute type fits best?
o: Memory-optimized instances with few cores
Memory helps some jobs, but training is limited by parallel compute.
Burstable general-purpose instances
They run out of CPU credits under steady load.
Storage-optimized instances with local NVMe
Fast disk doesn't speed up the math.
GPU-accelerated instances
Right. GPUs run many parallel operations, ideal for training models.

q.q: Users far from the region see slow page loads for images and scripts, but the servers are not busy. What helps most?
o: A CDN to cache static content near users
Right. The delay is distance (latency); caching at the edge fixes it.
Vertical scaling of the load balancer and the web servers
The load balancer isn't overloaded.
A larger database instance
Static files don't come from the database.
More web servers in the same region
Server capacity isn't the problem.

q.q: A factory has thousands of sensors sending small readings over unreliable links to the cloud. Which protocol is designed for this?
o: LDAP
LDAP is for directories.
SMTP
SMTP is for email.
RDP
RDP is for remote desktops.
MQTT
Right. MQTT is a lightweight publish/subscribe protocol built for IoT devices and weak links.

q.q: A company wants to add sentiment analysis to support tickets without training its own model. What should it use?
o: A provider's managed AI/ML service for language analysis
Right. Pre-trained managed services offer features like sentiment analysis through an API.
A CDN with edge caching rules
CDNs don't analyze text.
A relational database with a sentiment column filled in by the agents
A column doesn't analyze text.
A new GPU cluster to train a custom model from scratch
Possible, but far more work than needed.

q.q: IoT cameras must flag motion locally and only send alerts to the cloud, to save bandwidth. What is this approach?
o: Cloud bursting
That moves extra load to the cloud.
Edge computing
Right. Processing happens near the device, and only results go to the cloud.
Cold storage tiering
That's about storing data cheaply.
Lift and shift
That's a migration strategy.

q.q: Several government agencies share cloud infrastructure built for their common compliance needs, run by one provider. Which deployment model is this?
o: Hybrid cloud linking on-premises and public
Hybrid mixes environments; this is one shared environment.
Community cloud
Right. A community cloud serves organizations with shared requirements.
Public cloud open to any customer
Public clouds serve anyone, not a defined group.
Private cloud for a single agency
A private cloud serves one organization.

q.q: A company keeps sensitive records in its own data center but runs its website in a public cloud, with the two connected. What model is this?
o: Hybrid cloud
Right. Hybrid combines private (on-premises) and public cloud, working together.
Private cloud only
The website is in a public cloud.
Multicloud across two public providers
Multicloud uses several public providers; here one side is on premises.
Community cloud shared with partners
Nothing is shared with other organizations.

q.q: A bank must keep full control of hardware, but wants self-service VMs and automation for its teams. Which model fits?
o: SaaS from a banking software vendor
SaaS is a finished app, not self-service VMs.
Community cloud with other banks
Shared with others, so not full control.
Private cloud on premises
Right. A private cloud gives cloud features on hardware the bank controls.
Public cloud with reserved instances
Reservations don't give hardware control.

q.q: A company runs workloads in two different public cloud providers to avoid depending on one. What is this?
o: Community cloud
Community clouds are shared by a group of organizations.
Hybrid cloud
Hybrid mixes private and public.
Multicloud
Right. Using more than one public provider is multicloud.
Cloud bursting
Bursting overflows load to the cloud during peaks.

q.q: A team wants to release a new version to 5% of users first and expand only if errors stay low. Which strategy is this?
o: In-place deployment
In-place updates the existing servers directly.
Canary deployment
Right. A small group gets the new version first; rollout grows if it's healthy.
Blue-green deployment
Blue-green switches all traffic between two full environments at once.
A big-bang cutover over a weekend
Everyone gets the change at once.

q.q: A team runs two full production environments. It deploys to the idle one, tests it, then switches all traffic. Rollback is switching back. What is this?
o: In-place deployment
In-place changes the live servers themselves.
Rolling deployment
Rolling updates servers a few at a time in one environment.
Canary deployment
Canary sends a small share of traffic first.
Blue-green deployment
Right. Two identical environments; traffic flips between them.

q.q: An app runs on 10 servers. The team updates two at a time while the rest keep serving, until all are updated. What strategy is this?
o: Rolling deployment
Right. Batches are updated in turn so the service stays up.
Canary deployment
Canary is about a small share of users first, then decide.
Blue-green deployment
Blue-green needs a second full environment.
Lift and shift
That's a migration approach.

q.q: A small internal tool can be down for an hour at night, and the team has no spare servers. Which strategy is simplest?
o: In-place deployment during a maintenance window
Right. Updating the existing servers is simplest when downtime is allowed.
Multicloud active-active
Far more than needed.
Canary with traffic splitting
Adds complexity a small tool doesn't need.
Blue-green, with a second full environment built for the release
Needs spare capacity the team doesn't have.

q.q: A company must move 300 VMs to the cloud in three months with as few changes as possible. Which strategy fits?
o: Repurchase every app as SaaS
Not every app has a SaaS replacement, and it changes how users work.
Retire every app and start over
That stops the business.
Rehost (lift and shift)
Right. Moving workloads as-is is fastest and needs the fewest changes.
Refactor every app into microservices
That takes far longer than three months.

q.q: During migration, a team moves its database from a self-managed VM to the provider's managed database, with no code changes. Which strategy is this?
o: Replatform
Right. A small change to use a managed service, without re-architecting.
Retain on premises
Retain means leaving it where it is.
Rehost
Rehost would keep the database on a VM as-is.
Refactor
Refactoring changes the app's architecture.

q.q: A company must move 400 TB to the cloud, but its internet link would take months. What should it use?
o: Move the data with SFTP overnight, every night, until it's done
Still limited by the same link.
Compress the data with ZIP before uploading it
Helps a little, but not from months to days.
An offline transfer appliance shipped to the provider
Right. Physical transfer devices move large data sets faster than a slow link.
A bigger site-to-site VPN tunnel
The link speed is the limit, not the tunnel.

q.q: After migrating, a legacy app fails because it expects a server at a hard-coded on-premises IP. What should the migration plan have included?
o: Larger VM sizes for the migrated app and its database
Size doesn't fix a missing dependency.
A different cloud region
Region doesn't help reach an on-premises IP.
A dependency map of every system the app talks to
Right. Mapping dependencies before moving shows what else must move or be reachable.
A longer backup retention policy
Backups don't create missing dependencies.

q.q: Someone changed a security group in the console, and now it no longer matches the Terraform code. What is this called and how is it found?
o: A race condition, found by load testing the network
This isn't a timing issue.
Version skew, found by restarting the VMs in order
Restarts don't compare state.
Data sovereignty, found by a compliance scan
Unrelated to config changes.
Configuration drift, found with a plan or drift detection
Right. Comparing real state with the code reveals out-of-band changes.

q.q: Which file format is most commonly used for Kubernetes manifests and Ansible playbooks?
o: CSV
CSV is for tables of data.
Binary protobuf files
Not used for these files.
INI files only
INI is too simple for these structures.
YAML
Right. Both use YAML for readable, indented configuration.

q.q: A script must create a storage bucket only if it doesn't exist, so running it twice causes no errors or duplicates. What property is this?
o: Elasticity
Elasticity is about scaling resources up and down.
Idempotency
Right. Running the same code again gives the same result with no extra changes.
Immutability
Immutable means replaced rather than changed; it's related but not this.
Latency
Latency is about delay.

q.q: A team keeps its infrastructure code in Git. A change broke the network. What lets them recover fastest?
o: Revert to the last good commit and re-apply
Right. Versioned IaC lets you roll back to a known-good state.
Open a support ticket with the provider
The provider didn't make the change.
Delete the Git history to start fresh
That removes the good version.
Rebuild the network by hand in the console from memory
Slow and error-prone.

q.q: Requirements say: health data must stay in the country, be encrypted, and the app must survive a zone failure. Which choice meets all three?
o: An in-country region, encryption with managed keys, and multiple zones
Right. Location meets sovereignty, keys meet encryption and zones meet availability.
One zone in country with a larger instance size
Doesn't survive a zone failure.
An in-country region with public storage for speed
Public storage breaks the security requirement.
The cheapest region abroad, with encrypted backups copied to a second region
Data would leave the country.

q.q: A workload needs steady high disk throughput for a 2 TB database and predictable latency. Which provisioning choice fits?
o: Archive object storage
Archive tiers are for rare access.
Standard HDD block storage
HDDs are slow for databases.
Provisioned-IOPS SSD block storage
Right. Provisioned IOPS guarantees steady performance.
Instance ephemeral (local NVMe) storage
Data is lost when the instance stops.

q.q: A web app must stay within a fixed monthly budget and handle occasional spikes. What provisioning choice balances both?
o: Autoscaling with a minimum and maximum instance count and budget alerts
Right. Limits cap cost while scaling covers spikes; alerts warn early.
A single small instance with no scaling
Spikes would take it down.
Unlimited autoscaling with no maximum instance count
Cost can run away during a spike or attack.
Fixed large instances sized for the biggest spike of the year
Wastes budget most of the month.

q.q: A team must provision a VM that only internal users reach. Which network setting is right?
o: A public subnet with a public IP and a strong, rotated admin password
Exposes the VM to the internet.
A private subnet with no public IP, reached through VPN or private access
Right. No public exposure while internal users can still connect.
A public IP with port 3389 open to everyone
Exposes RDP to the internet.
Any subnet with a public IP, since the cloud firewall denies inbound by default
Defaults vary; you should choose private placement.

q.q: A request passes through six microservices and sometimes takes 9 seconds. Which tool shows which service adds the delay?
o: A port scan of each service
That shows open ports, not timing.
A daily export of every service's logs to storage
Too slow and not linked across services.
Distributed tracing
Right. Traces follow one request across services and time each step.
CPU graphs for each host
They show load, not where a single request waits.

q.q: An alert fires every time CPU touches 80% for one second, and the team now ignores it. What is the best fix?
o: Alert only when CPU stays high for several minutes
Right. A sustained threshold cuts noise from brief spikes.
Delete the CPU alert entirely
Real problems would be missed.
Send the alert to more people
More people ignoring the same noise.
Lower the threshold to 50% so problems are caught earlier
That fires even more often.

q.q: Which of these is a metric rather than a log?
o: A trace ID linking six services
That's tracing data.
A line saying 'user jsmith logged in at 10:02'
That's a log entry describing an event.
Average response time per minute
Right. Metrics are numeric measurements over time.
A stack trace from an app crash
Also a log entry.

q.q: A team wants logs from 200 servers searchable in one place for 90 days. What should they set up?
o: Email alerts for every log line
Floods inboxes and isn't storage.
Weekly screenshots of each server's log viewer
Not searchable.
Keep longer log files on each of the 200 servers
Still scattered across 200 servers.
Centralized log aggregation with a retention policy
Right. Shipping logs to one store makes them searchable; retention keeps 90 days.

q.q: An on-call engineer gets an alert at 3 a.m. What should the alert include to speed triage?
o: The affected service, severity, a dashboard link and a runbook link
Right. Context and next steps help the engineer act quickly.
The full raw log file from every server attached to the page
Too much to read in an emergency.
A list of every server in the company
Not focused on the problem.
Only the word 'ERROR' so the page is short
No context to act on.

q.q: A ticketing site always gets heavy traffic at 9 a.m. on Mondays. Which scaling approach fits best?
o: Manual scaling after users complain
Too late and needs someone awake.
Vertical scaling of one server each Monday
Needs downtime and has limits.
No scaling, since spikes are short
Users would get errors every Monday.
Scheduled scaling before 9 a.m. on Mondays
Right. Known patterns can be handled by adding capacity ahead of time.

q.q: Which change is horizontal scaling?
o: Adding RAM to the existing server
Also vertical.
Moving the app to an instance with more vCPUs and memory
That's vertical scaling.
Upgrading the existing server's disk to SSD
That changes one server's resources.
Adding three more instances behind the load balancer
Right. Horizontal scaling adds more instances.

q.q: An autoscaling group adds instances when CPU is over 70%, but new instances take 8 minutes to be ready, and users see errors meanwhile. What should be tuned?
o: Raise the scale-out threshold to 95% CPU
That scales even later.
Remove the health checks so new instances get traffic sooner
Unhealthy instances would get traffic.
Set the maximum to the current size
That stops scaling.
Pre-baked images and a lower scale-out threshold or warm pool
Right. Faster boot and earlier scaling cover the gap.

q.q: Why might vertical scaling be a poor choice for a busy web tier?
o: It needs downtime to resize and has a hard size limit
Right. You can only grow one instance so far, often with a restart.
It requires a load balancer
Vertical scaling doesn't need one.
It always costs more than adding instances
Not a reason it's poor, and not always true.
It spreads load across many servers, which adds latency
That's horizontal scaling.

q.q: A queue-based worker pool should grow when work piles up. Which trigger fits best?
o: The number of messages waiting in the queue
Right. Queue depth directly measures the backlog of work.
The amount of free disk space on each worker
Disk size doesn't reflect backlog.
The time of day only
Workload may not match the clock.
The number of DNS queries
Unrelated to queue work.

q.q: Ransomware encrypted servers and also deleted the backups reachable from the network. Which backup feature would have prevented losing them?
o: Compressing backups before storing them
Compressed backups can still be deleted.
More frequent incremental backups
They would be deleted the same way.
Immutable or air-gapped backup copies
Right. Copies that can't be changed or reached from the network survive the attack.
Faster backup storage
Speed doesn't protect against deletion.

q.q: A full backup runs Sunday. Each weekday backs up only changes since Sunday's full. To restore Thursday, which sets are needed?
o: Sunday's full plus every day Monday to Thursday
That's how incremental backups restore.
Sunday's full plus Thursday's backup
Right. These are differential backups: each holds every change since the last full.
Only Sunday's full backup
That misses the week's changes.
Only Thursday's backup
A differential needs the full backup too.

q.q: A team has backed up a database nightly for a year but never restored one. What is the biggest risk?
o: Too many people know the backup schedule
Not the main risk.
Backup storage is too cheap
Cost isn't the risk.
The backups may not actually restore
Right. Untested backups can be corrupt or incomplete; test restores prove they work.
The restores will run faster than expected
Speed isn't the risk; whether they work at all is.

q.q: A database must be recoverable to any minute in the last 7 days. Which feature provides this?
o: A weekly full backup only
You could only go back to the weekly copy.
A VM snapshot taken once a day at midnight
Only daily restore points.
Point-in-time recovery using transaction logs
Right. Logs replayed on top of a backup reach any moment in the window.
RAID 1 mirroring on the database's disks
RAID protects against disk failure, not bad changes.

q.q: Backups are stored in the same region as production. A regional outage would affect both. What should be added?
o: Cross-region replication of the backups
Right. A copy in another region survives a regional outage.
Longer retention of the backups in the same region
Still lost with the region.
A second backup job in the same zone
Same failure domain.
Encryption of the backups
Good practice, but doesn't help availability.

q.q: Old project VMs still run months after the project ended, costing money and missing patches. What process fixes this?
o: Decommissioning with owner tags, expiry dates and regular reviews
Right. Knowing who owns what and when it ends lets you retire it safely.
Patch the old VMs more often so they stay compliant
They cost money for no purpose.
Take snapshots and keep everything running
Doesn't retire anything.
Move them to a cheaper region and shut them down at night
They'd still cost money and still serve no purpose.

q.q: Before deleting a storage volume with customer data, what must happen?
o: Confirm retention rules, then securely delete it and record it
Right. Retention requirements come first, then sanitization with a record.
Delete it immediately to save money and reduce exposure
May break retention rules.
Make it public for a week so customers can download their data
That exposes the data.
Rename it to 'old' and leave it
Data stays exposed and costs money.

q.q: A team patches cloud VMs by logging in to each one. What is a better life-cycle approach?
o: Give every developer admin rights to patch
Inconsistent and risky.
Build patched golden images and replace instances on a schedule
Right. Immutable images make every instance consistent and current.
Log in to each VM monthly and patch only critical flaws
Still manual, slow and inconsistent, and it leaves many flaws open.
Turn off automatic updates everywhere to avoid surprise reboots
Creates more unpatched systems.

q.q: Object storage holds logs that must move to cheaper tiers after 30 days and be deleted after 1 year. What should be set?
o: A weekly script someone runs by hand
Easy to forget.
A storage life-cycle policy
Right. Life-cycle rules move and delete objects automatically by age.
Versioning on the bucket
Versioning keeps more copies, not fewer.
A larger bucket
Size doesn't move or delete objects.

q.q: A provider announces that a VM instance type will be retired next year. What should the team do?
o: Wait until the instances stop working, then resize them
That causes an outage.
Buy more of the retiring type now
They'll still be retired.
Ignore it, since cloud resources never change
Providers retire things regularly.
Plan a move to a supported type before the date
Right. Life-cycle management includes acting on provider deprecations.

q.q: A scan finds 600 vulnerabilities across the cloud estate. What should decide which ones are fixed first?
o: Whichever team is least busy
Workload doesn't measure risk.
Severity plus exposure and asset importance
Right. A critical flaw on an internet-facing production system beats one on an isolated test box.
The oldest findings first, whatever their severity
Age alone ignores impact.
The order the scanner listed them in
Scanner order isn't risk.

q.q: What does a CVE identifier give a cloud team?
o: A standard name for a specific known vulnerability
Right. CVE IDs let tools and teams refer to the same flaw.
A list of attackers using the flaw
That's threat intelligence.
A score that measures how severe the flaw is
That's CVSS.
A patch that the scanner can apply to fix the flaw automatically
CVEs don't include fixes.

q.q: A scanner reports a flaw in a library, but the team confirms that code path is never used. What should they do?
o: Document it as a false positive or accepted risk, with a review date
Right. Record the reasoning so it isn't lost and gets rechecked.
Turn off the scanner for that host
Hides future real findings.
Delete the finding from the scanner so the report is clean
Loses the reasoning and the trail.
Ignore every finding in that library from now on
Future real flaws would be missed.

q.q: Container images are scanned once at build time, but new CVEs appear weekly. What should be added?
o: Build images less often so they're scanned fewer times
That leaves them unpatched longer.
Delete and recreate the registry after each release
You'd lose the images you run.
Continuous rescanning of images in the registry and running workloads
Right. New CVEs affect images that were clean when built.
Scan only the base OS, not the app
App dependencies carry many flaws.

q.q: A law requires citizens' data to be stored and processed only within the country. Which concept is this?
o: Data tiering
That moves data between storage classes.
Data deduplication
That reduces storage use.
Data sovereignty and locality
Right. Data must stay under the laws of, and inside, a given country.
Data classification and labeling
Classification labels sensitivity, not location.

q.q: A cloud provider's customers ask for proof its controls are audited. Which report fits best for security controls?
o: A pen test from the provider's own staff
Not independent assurance.
A marketing brochure about security
Not evidence.
A SOC 2 report
Right. SOC 2 audits security, availability and confidentiality controls.
A SOC 1 report
SOC 1 covers controls over customers' financial reporting.

q.q: Records must be kept seven years and then deleted. Which control enforces this in cloud storage?
o: Encrypting the records with customer-managed keys
Encryption doesn't control retention.
Moving records to a faster tier
Tiering doesn't enforce retention.
Manual deletion by the records team when someone remembers
Manual steps get forgotten, so records are kept too long or deleted too early.
A retention policy with automatic deletion after seven years
Right. Policies enforce both keeping and deleting on time.

q.q: Who owns customer data stored in a public cloud under a typical agreement?
o: The cloud provider
Providers don't take ownership of customer data.
The government of the region
Location affects law, not ownership.
The customer
Right. The provider stores and processes it; ownership stays with the customer.
Whoever has admin access
Access isn't ownership.

q.q: Admins log in to the cloud console with only a password. What is the most important change?
o: Hide the console URL
Obscurity isn't protection.
Require MFA for every admin
Right. MFA stops most attacks with stolen passwords.
Make passwords expire every 30 days
Frequent changes alone don't stop phishing.
Share one admin account among the team
Breaks accountability.

q.q: An app running on a VM needs to read a database secret. What is the best way to give it access?
o: Put the cloud admin's access keys in the app's config file
Leaks admin power.
Make the secret store public
Exposes the secret.
Hard-code the secret in the source code and keep the repo private
Ends up in Git and images.
Assign the VM a managed identity or role with read access to that secret
Right. No stored keys, and access is scoped.

q.q: An auditor asks who deleted a storage bucket last week. What makes this answerable?
o: Encryption at rest on the bucket
Encryption doesn't record actions.
Audit trail logs of API activity kept centrally
Right. Cloud audit logs record who did what, when and from where.
A larger storage quota for the logging bucket
More space doesn't record who did what.
Bucket versioning turned on for every bucket
Versioning keeps object copies, not who deleted the bucket.

q.q: Which is an example of authorization rather than authentication?
o: A certificate proves the device's identity
Authentication.
A policy allows the user to read but not delete objects
Right. Authorization decides what an authenticated user may do.
A federated login from a partner's IdP
Still authentication.
The user enters a password and then an MFA code
That proves identity: authentication.

q.q: A database password appears in a Git repository. What is the best long-term fix?
o: Delete the commit from Git history and keep the same password
The password is already exposed.
Base64-encode the password in the code
Encoding isn't protection.
Store secrets in a secrets manager and rotate the leaked one
Right. Rotate now; then keep secrets out of code with a vault.
Make the repository private
People and tools may already have copies.

q.q: A team wants a standard checklist of secure settings for its cloud accounts. What should it use?
o: A recognized benchmark such as the CIS benchmarks
Right. Benchmarks give tested, specific hardening settings.
Settings copied from a popular forum post
Forum advice isn't tested or maintained like a benchmark.
Whatever the newest engineer prefers
Not a standard.
The provider's default settings, left unchanged after setup
Defaults are often not hardened.

q.q: Containers in a cluster run as root with full Linux capabilities. Which change follows best practice?
o: Give containers host networking and keep root for compatibility
Increases exposure.
Disable image scanning to speed builds
Removes a control.
Run as non-root, drop capabilities and use read-only file systems
Right. Limits what an attacker gains if a container is compromised.
Mount the host's root file system so logs are easy to collect
Gives the container the host.

q.q: Which approach reflects zero trust in a cloud environment?
o: Check identity only once per day
Not continuous verification.
Allow all traffic between subnets inside the same VPC
Implicit trust inside the network.
Trust anything coming from the corporate VPN or office network
That's perimeter trust.
Verify every request by identity and context, even from inside the VPC
Right. Location inside the network doesn't grant trust.

q.q: An internet-facing web app is hit by a large flood of traffic from many sources. Which cloud control helps most?
o: A stronger admin password on the cloud console
Unrelated to traffic floods.
Encrypting the database
Doesn't stop floods.
A larger log retention period
Records the attack, doesn't stop it.
A managed DDoS protection service
Right. It absorbs and filters floods before they reach the app.

q.q: Security wants to stop employees uploading files labeled Confidential to personal cloud storage. Which control fits?
o: An intrusion detection system
IDS looks for attacks, not data policy.
A load balancer
Balances traffic; no data inspection.
Autoscaling the web tier
Scaling doesn't inspect or block file uploads.
Data loss prevention (DLP)
Right. DLP inspects content and labels and can block the transfer.

q.q: A security group allows SSH from 0.0.0.0/0 to every VM. What is the best fix?
o: Disable logging on the security group
Removes visibility.
Open every other port too for consistency
More exposure.
Move SSH to port 2222 and keep it open to 0.0.0.0/0
Scanners find other ports.
Allow SSH only from the bastion or admin IP range
Right. Restrict the source to what needs it.

q.q: A team wants to detect known exploit patterns in network traffic to its VMs and block them automatically. Which control fits?
o: An IDS in passive mode on a mirror port
An IDS alerts but doesn't block.
A CDN
CDNs cache content.
A NAT gateway
NAT translates addresses.
An intrusion prevention system (IPS)
Right. An IPS inspects traffic for attack patterns and blocks them inline.

q.q: Cloud logs show an access key created at 2 a.m. and then used from an unusual country to start 40 large GPU instances. What attack does this suggest?
o: A DNS outage that forced instances to restart
DNS problems don't create access keys or start GPU instances.
A routine backup job
Backups don't start GPU instances.
A normal autoscaling event
Autoscaling doesn't create keys or come from new countries.
Stolen credentials used for cryptomining
Right. Unexpected keys and sudden GPU instances are classic signs of account takeover for mining.

q.q: Monitoring shows a VM suddenly listening on port 4444, which it never used before. What should happen first?
o: Add 4444 to the allowed list in every security group
Spreads the exposure.
Ignore it, since apps change ports when they update
Unexpected listeners can be backdoors.
Reboot the load balancer in front of the VM
The load balancer isn't involved in a new listener on the VM.
Investigate the process behind it as a possible backdoor
Right. A new unexpected listener is a deviation from baseline worth checking.

q.q: A storage bucket shows thousands of GET requests from one IP listing every object in an hour. What does this suggest?
o: Data exfiltration or scraping of a misconfigured bucket
Right. Mass listing and download from one source is a red flag.
A routine life-cycle policy
Life-cycle rules don't download objects.
A healthy autoscaling event adding new instances
Autoscaling adds compute; it doesn't list and download every object.
A normal CDN cache refresh
CDNs come from many edge IPs and known ranges.

q.q: Many failed logins hit different user accounts, each with one or two tries, from many IPs. What attack is this?
o: Password spraying
Right. Few common passwords across many accounts avoids lockouts.
A man-in-the-middle attack
Not a login-guessing pattern.
A brute force on one account
That's many tries on one account.
A SQL injection attack
That targets queries.

q.q: A developer wants to build a new feature without affecting the main code until it's reviewed. What should they do?
o: Commit straight to main and fix any breakage later
Unreviewed changes can break everyone.
Email the changed files to the team lead
No history or review trail.
Create a branch and open a pull request when ready
Right. Branches isolate work; pull requests get review before merging.
Copy the whole repository into a new folder
Loses version control benefits.

q.q: Two developers changed the same line in different branches. What happens when the second one merges?
o: The newest commit silently wins
Git doesn't silently overwrite.
A merge conflict that someone must resolve
Right. Git can't pick a winner automatically when both changed the same line.
Git keeps both lines side by side automatically
It marks a conflict instead.
The repository is deleted
Nothing is deleted.

q.q: What is the main purpose of a code review on a pull request?
o: Catch bugs and security problems before code is merged
Right. Another set of eyes finds issues early.
Replace the need for automated unit and integration tests
Reviews and tests complement each other.
Back up the repository
Reviews aren't backups.
Make the build run faster
Reviews don't speed builds.

q.q: Every commit should be built and tested automatically, and failures should block the merge. Which practice is this?
o: Continuous integration (CI)
Right. CI builds and tests each change as it's committed.
Blue-green deployment
That's a release strategy.
Continuous deployment
That's about releasing automatically after tests pass.
Infrastructure as code
That's about defining infrastructure in code.

q.q: A pipeline builds a container image once and promotes the exact same image from test to production. Why?
o: So production runs the artifact that was tested
Right. Rebuilding could change what runs.
To keep a separate copy of every image for each stage
The point is to reuse one image, not keep copies.
Because Git doesn't allow the same image to be rebuilt twice
Git doesn't decide this.
Because production can't build images
Production could build them; rebuilding risks changing what runs.

q.q: Where should a pipeline get the cloud credentials it needs to deploy?
o: Printed in the build log for debugging
Logs leak them.
Short-lived credentials from the pipeline's secret store or identity federation
Right. Keeps secrets out of code and limits their lifetime.
A senior developer's personal access keys with admin rights
Tied to one person and too broad.
Hard-coded in the pipeline YAML file in the repository
Ends up in the repository.

q.q: A web front end needs to request only the specific fields it needs from many backend objects in one call. Which API style fits?
o: SMTP
SMTP sends email.
SOAP
SOAP uses fixed XML messages, not client-chosen fields.
FTP
FTP transfers files.
GraphQL
Right. Clients ask for exactly the fields they want in one query.

q.q: A chat app needs the server to push new messages to the browser instantly over a long-lived connection. Which technology fits?
o: A batch file transfer to the browser every night
Not real time.
REST polling every 10 minutes
Far from instant.
DNS TXT records
Not a messaging channel.
WebSockets
Right. WebSockets keep a two-way connection open for real-time messages.

q.q: Which describes an event-driven architecture?
o: Services react to events like 'order placed' instead of calling each other directly
Right. Producers publish events; consumers react independently.
A user manually starting each step
Manual, not event-driven.
A single program that calls each service in order and waits for each reply
That's a monolith.
A nightly batch job that runs every step for the day's orders at once
Scheduled, not event-driven.

q.q: Which tool is mainly used to define cloud infrastructure as code across many providers?
o: Terraform
Right. Terraform declares infrastructure in code and applies it to many providers.
Docker
Docker builds and runs containers.
Jenkins
Jenkins runs CI/CD jobs.
Grafana
Grafana builds dashboards.

q.q: A team wants dashboards of metrics from several data sources. Which tool fits?
o: Grafana
Right. Grafana visualizes metrics from many sources.
Git
Git tracks code changes.
Kubernetes
Kubernetes orchestrates containers.
Ansible
Ansible automates configuration.

q.q: A team must apply the same settings to 300 servers with agentless automation over SSH. Which tool fits?
o: Ansible
Right. Ansible pushes configuration over SSH with no agent needed.
Grafana
Dashboards only.
Kubernetes
Kubernetes runs containers, not server config.
The ELK stack
Logging and search.

q.q: A Terraform apply fails with 'quota exceeded for vCPUs in region'. What is the fix?
o: Change the instance's DNS name and retry
DNS names don't affect vCPU quotas.
Delete and recreate the Terraform state file
State isn't the problem, and deleting it would make Terraform lose track of resources.
Open port 443 on the instance's security group
Network rules don't affect quotas.
Request a quota increase or deploy fewer or smaller instances
Right. The account hit its resource limit in that region.

q.q: A deployment works in one region but fails in another with 'instance type not supported'. What is the likely cause?
o: The first region is out of IP addresses for new subnets
That wouldn't affect the second region.
The second region needs a separate account
One account can use every region; the error says the type isn't supported.
The template is in YAML instead of JSON
Format isn't the issue.
That instance type isn't offered in the second region
Right. Services and sizes vary by region.

q.q: A new version deploys, but the app crashes because it needs a newer runtime than the base image provides. What type of issue is this?
o: A DNS propagation delay after the deployment
The app runs but crashes.
A DDoS attack
No attack involved.
An incompatibility between the app and its environment
Right. Version mismatch between code and runtime.
A backup failure during the deployment
Backups don't decide which runtime the image has.

q.q: After a deployment, the app can't connect to its database. The new config file has the old database host name. What is the issue?
o: The database ran out of storage
Then it would still be reachable.
A regional outage
Other services work.
A misconfiguration in the deployment
Right. Wrong settings in the deployed config.
Too many availability zones in the deployment
Zone count doesn't change the host name in the config.

q.q: A deployment fails because a storage bucket name is already taken. Why?
o: The account has MFA turned on for API calls
MFA doesn't block names.
Bucket names must be globally unique at many providers
Right. Another account already owns that name.
The account's region doesn't support object storage
Object storage is offered in every region; the error is about the name.
The VPC has too many subnets
Unrelated to bucket names.

q.q: A new VM gets an IP like 169.254.x.x and can't reach anything. What is the most likely cause?
o: It couldn't get an address from DHCP
Right. 169.254 is a self-assigned address used when DHCP fails.
Its security group blocks all outbound traffic
Security groups don't change the address; a 169.254 address comes from failed DHCP.
Its DNS server is wrong
DNS problems don't change the IP address.
Its NTP server is unreachable
Time sync doesn't set the IP.

q.q: A load balancer returns HTTP 502 Bad Gateway. What does that usually mean?
o: The user typed the wrong password at the login page
That's usually 401.
The client is not allowed to see the page
That's 403.
The load balancer got a bad or no response from the backend
Right. 502 points at the upstream server, not the client.
The page doesn't exist
That's 404.

q.q: Instances in a private subnet can't reach the internet for updates. The NAT gateway exists. What should be checked first?
o: The NAT gateway's instance size
Size affects throughput, not whether traffic reaches the NAT gateway at all.
The VMs' DNS resolver settings
DNS problems show up as name errors; timeouts to every host point at routing.
The private subnet's route table has a default route to the NAT gateway
Right. Without the route, traffic never reaches the NAT gateway.
The internet gateway attached to the public subnet
The NAT gateway uses it, but the private subnet still needs its own route to the NAT.

q.q: Two VPCs are peered, but traffic doesn't flow. Both have CIDR 10.0.0.0/16. What is the problem?
o: DNS resolution must be turned off in both VPCs
DNS settings don't block routing between peers.
Overlapping IP ranges can't be routed between peers
Right. Peering needs unique, non-overlapping CIDRs.
The VPCs need public IPs on every instance
Peering is private.
Peering only works between VPCs in different accounts
Peering works inside one account too.

q.q: Logins to a cloud service fail with 'token not yet valid' on some servers only. What should be checked?
o: The servers' TLS cipher suites
A cipher problem fails the TLS handshake, not token validity.
The servers' disk space for token caching
Tokens aren't rejected for disk space; the message is about time.
NTP time sync on those servers
Right. Tokens are time-based; skewed clocks make them look invalid.
The VLAN tag on the load balancer
A VLAN problem blocks traffic entirely; this error is about token time.

q.q: After a provider update, old clients can't connect to an API, and logs show 'no shared cipher'. What happened?
o: Old cipher suites or TLS versions were deprecated
Right. The server stopped offering the weak ciphers the old clients use.
The API's rate limit was lowered
Rate limits return HTTP 429, not 'no shared cipher'.
The clients' passwords expired before the update
Passwords come after the TLS handshake.
The API's DNS record was deleted
Then clients couldn't find it at all.

q.q: A developer gets 'AccessDenied' when writing to a bucket, though they can read it. What is the likely cause?
o: The region is down
Reads would also fail.
Their password is wrong or expired
They'd fail to log in at all.
The bucket is full
Errors would mention capacity.
Their policy allows read but not write actions
Right. Authorization covers each action separately.

q.q: A user who should have read-only access was able to delete VMs. What type of issue is this?
o: Privilege escalation or an over-permissive role
Right. The user has more rights than intended.
A DHCP failure on the user's VM
Network problems don't grant extra rights.
An expired MFA token
An expired token would block access, not give extra rights.
A cipher suite mismatch
Cipher issues block connections; they don't grant extra rights.

q.q: A scan finds unknown software running on several cloud VMs. What should happen first?
o: Add the software to the approved list so the scan passes
Approval needs review.
Reboot the VMs and close the ticket
A reboot doesn't remove it.
Leave them running while you check whether the VMs still work
Malware often runs quietly.
Investigate and isolate the affected VMs per the incident process
Right. Unauthorized software can be malware; contain it and investigate.

q.q: A cloud access key was found in a public GitHub repository. What is the first step?
o: Revoke or rotate the key immediately
Right. Bots scan GitHub constantly; disable the key before it's abused.
Wait to see if anyone uses it
Attackers act within minutes.
Delete the GitHub repository and do nothing else
The key is already copied and still works.
Email the team about it next week
Far too slow.

q.title: Pick the storage for each workload
q.scenario: A cloud team is placing five workloads. Pick the storage type and the tier for each one.

rows.req: A busy SQL database's data volume on one VM.
rows.why: Databases need low-latency block volumes on fast, hot storage.

rows.req: Audit logs kept seven years, read maybe once a year.
rows.why: Archive object storage is the cheapest place for rarely read data.

rows.req: Website images served to users all day through a CDN.
rows.why: Object storage is the usual CDN origin, and these are read constantly.

rows.req: A shared folder that 20 Linux VMs mount at the same time.
rows.why: NFS/SMB file storage handles shared access from many machines.

rows.req: Last quarter's project files, opened a few times a month.
rows.why: Cool object storage costs less for data that's read now and then.

q.title: Find the cause of each ticket
q.scenario: Five tickets came in overnight. Read each one and pick the most likely cause. Each answer is used once; two choices are distractors.

items.log:
ip addr: inet 169.254.33.10/16
ping 10.20.0.1: Destination Host Unreachable
items.why: A 169.254 address means the VM assigned itself one after DHCP got no answer.

items.log:
curl https://api.example.com -> Could not resolve host
curl https://93.184.215.14 -> 200 OK
items.why: Works by IP but not by name: name resolution is broken.

items.log:
yum update -> Connection timed out
route table: 10.20.0.0/16 local (no 0.0.0.0/0)
items.why: No default route to the NAT gateway, so internet traffic has nowhere to go.
The server's clock is behind, so a fresh assertion looks like it's from the future.

items.log:
Error: creating instance: VcpuLimitExceeded
Requested 8, current usage 62 of 64
items.why: The account hit its vCPU limit in the region.

q.title: Choose the deployment strategy
q.scenario: Pick the best deployment strategy for each release.

rows.req: A risky change to checkout; the team wants 2% of users first and to watch error rates.
rows.why: Canary exposes a small share of users before going wider.

rows.req: The team has budget for a full second environment and wants instant rollback by switching traffic.
rows.why: Blue-green keeps the old environment ready; rollback is a traffic switch.

rows.req: A 12-node web tier must stay up, with no spare environment, updating a few nodes at a time.
rows.why: Rolling updates batches while the others keep serving.

rows.req: An internal tool with an approved one-hour outage window and no spare servers.
rows.why: In-place is simplest when downtime is allowed.

q.title: Design the backups
q.scenario: For each requirement, pick the backup approach and where the copy should live.

rows.req: A database must be restorable to any minute in the past week, even if the region goes down.
rows.why: Transaction logs give any-minute recovery; another region survives a regional outage.

rows.req: Backups must survive ransomware that steals admin credentials.
rows.why: Copies that can't be changed or reached from the network can't be wiped by the attacker.

rows.req: A quick rollback point for a VM before a risky patch tonight.
rows.why: A snapshot right before the change is the fastest local rollback.

rows.req: A file server needs nightly backups with low storage use and a copy outside the region.
rows.why: A weekly full with nightly incrementals saves space; keep a copy in another region.
